root.note: Built on mandere, ‘to chew’. The TLFi links it to Manducus, a greedy figure of Roman comedy.

history: Latin had a verb for ‘to eat’, edere, but it was short and irregular, and some of its forms sounded like forms of esse, ‘to be’. Ordinary speakers preferred something more vivid: manducare, ‘to chew, to munch’, from mandere, ‘to chew’. The TLFi links it to Manducus, a greedy figure of Roman comedy, so the word meant something like ‘to work your jaws’. From the 1st century AD, comedere was the polite word and manducare the popular one. French, Provençal and Romanian took the popular one: manger, manjà, mânca. Spanish and Portuguese took the polite one: comer. Manger is already in a French text from the end of the 10th century. One spelling trap: nous mangeons keeps an e, so that the g stays soft.
historyEinfach: Manger comes from the Latin verb manducare. It meant ‘to chew’. The normal Latin verb for ‘to eat’ was short and difficult, so people used manducare instead. Spanish took another Latin verb: comer. Spelling tip: nous mangeons, with an e after the g.

elsewhere.text: Spanish and Portuguese comer come from comedere, the polite Latin word. French chose the popular, chewing one.
